questions.stem: Enzymes belong to which class of substances?
questions.why: Enzymes belong to a class of substances called catalysts. They make chemical reactions possible by forming and breaking chemical bonds.

options.why: That is what an enzyme acts upon.
Those regulate pH rather than speed reactions.
Those release ions in water.

questions.stem: What defines a catalyst?
questions.why: A catalyst speeds up the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed. That is why a single enzyme can drive the same reaction over and over.

options.t: Speeds a reaction and is consumed by it
options.why: A catalyst emerges unchanged and can act again.

options.t: Speeds a reaction without being consumed
Slows a reaction to a controllable rate
options.why: Catalysts speed reactions rather than slow them.

options.t: Supplies the energy a reaction requires
options.why: Catalysts lower the energy needed but do not supply it.

questions.stem: What is the pocket on an enzyme's surface where a reaction takes place called?
questions.why: The active site is the special pocket on the enzyme's surface. The molecule that fits into it is the substrate, and what gets released afterward is the product.

options.why: That is the molecule that fits into the pocket.
Receptor sites belong to membrane proteins.
That is what emerges after the reaction.

questions.stem: In enzyme activity, what is the substrate?
questions.why: The substrate is the molecule the enzyme is supposed to react with; it fits right inside the active site pocket. What comes out afterward is the product.

options.t: The molecule that blocks the enzyme
options.why: That is an inhibitor.
That is the product.

options.t: The molecule the enzyme acts upon
The pocket where the reaction occurs
options.why: That is the active site.

questions.stem: After an enzyme completes its reaction, the new molecule or substance released is called what?
questions.why: Active site, then substrate, then product — that is the sequence. The enzyme itself is unchanged and moves on to the next substrate.

options.why: That is what entered the reaction.
That blocks the reaction rather than resulting from it.
That is the enzyme itself, which is unchanged.

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of enzyme activity in the body?
questions.why: Enzymes help build muscle, destroy toxins, metabolize drugs, form proteins, and break down food particles during digestion. Oxygen transport is a red blood cell function.

options.t: Conducting an impulse along a nerve fiber
options.why: That is a nervous system function.

options.t: Carrying oxygen from the lungs to the tissues
options.why: That is a red blood cell function.

options.t: Breaking down food particles during digestion

options.why: Storage is a metabolic rather than enzymatic example.

questions.stem: How does increasing temperature generally affect the rate of an enzyme reaction?
questions.why: Higher temperature means a faster reaction — but temperature can become so high that enzymes are unable to work at all. This is why a febrile patient burns through sedation medication faster.

options.t: Faster, with no upper temperature limit
options.why: There is an upper limit beyond which enzymes stop.

options.t: Slower, until heat halts enzymes entirely
options.why: Reactions accelerate with heat until enzymes fail.

options.t: Faster, until heat halts enzymes entirely

options.why: Enzymes have no self-regulating mechanism.

questions.stem: A patient presents with a significant fever. Based on the effect of temperature on enzyme activity, what should you anticipate about their drug metabolism?
questions.why: Enzyme reactions run faster at higher temperatures, and drug metabolism is enzyme-driven. A febrile patient metabolizes sedation faster, so it wears off sooner.

options.why: Enzyme-driven metabolism accelerates with heat.

options.t: Medications will not work at all
options.why: Medications still work, just for a shorter time.
Temperature directly affects enzyme activity.

questions.stem: What effect do alkalosis and acidosis have on enzyme reactions?
questions.why: Both a high pH (alkalosis) and a low pH (acidosis) typically slow the reaction or even stop it. Enzymes work within a narrow pH window, which is part of why acid-base derangement is so dangerous.

options.t: Neither has any effect as long as temperature is normal
options.why: pH affects enzymes independently of temperature.

options.t: Both typically slow the reaction or stop it entirely
Alkalosis speeds reactions while acidosis slows them
options.why: Alkalosis slows reactions rather than speeding them.

options.t: Acidosis speeds reactions while alkalosis slows them
options.why: Acidosis slows reactions rather than speeding them.

questions.stem: What is an enzyme inhibitor?
questions.why: Inhibitors are molecules specially made to stop the activity of enzymes, and in some cases simply slow them down.

options.t: A molecule specifically made to stop or slow the activity of an enzyme
A rise in temperature that denatures the enzyme
options.why: Heat denaturing is a temperature effect, not an inhibitor.

options.t: A molecule that binds to the active site and is converted into product
options.why: That describes a substrate being converted.

options.t: A buffer that stabilizes the enzyme's pH environment
options.why: Buffers stabilize pH rather than block enzymes.

questions.stem: Which four factors are listed as affecting enzyme activity?
questions.why: Temperature, pH, concentration, and inhibitors. Higher concentration increases reaction rate; inhibitors decrease or stop it.

options.t: pH level, hydration, blood flow, and inhibitors
options.why: Hydration and blood flow are not among the four.
Pressure and volume are not among the four listed.

options.t: Concentration, oxygen level, glucose level, and temperature
options.why: Oxygen and glucose levels are not among the four.

options.t: Temperature, pH level, concentration, and inhibitors

questions.stem: How are electrolytes defined?
questions.why: Electrolytes are substances that release ions in water. The resulting electrically charged particles are what conduct electricity.

options.why: That describes bases specifically.

options.t: Proteins that carry charge across cell membranes
options.why: Membrane proteins carry charge but are not electrolytes.

options.t: Substances that dissolve fats in water
options.why: Lipids are not water-soluble by definition.

options.t: Substances that release ions in water

questions.stem: What happens when an electrolyte dissolves in water?
questions.why: The negative and positive ends of water molecules pull the ions apart so they interact with water rather than with each other. The result is charged particles in solution that conduct electricity.

options.t: Water binds the ions into neutral pairs
options.why: Water pulls the ions apart rather than pairing them.

options.t: Water pulls the ions apart from each other
The electrolyte settles out as a solid
options.why: Dissolving is the opposite of precipitating out.

options.t: Water splits into hydrogen and oxygen
options.why: Water molecules remain intact.

questions.stem: How is an acid defined?
questions.why: Acids release hydrogen ions in water — citric acid and lactic acid are the examples given. Bases do the opposite: they release ions that bond with hydrogen ions.

options.t: Any substance with a pH above 7
options.why: pH above 7 describes a base.

options.t: A compound that resists changes in pH
options.why: That describes a buffer.

options.t: An electrolyte that releases ions which bond with hydrogen ions
options.why: That defines a base.

options.t: An electrolyte that releases hydrogen ions in water

questions.stem: Bleach and ammonia are given as examples of which type of substance?
questions.why: Bases are electrolytes that release ions which bond with hydrogen ions; bleach and ammonia are the examples. Citric and lactic acid are the acid examples.

options.why: Citric and lactic acid are the acid examples.
Buffers resist pH change rather than causing it.
Both release ions in water, so both are electrolytes.

questions.stem: The acidity or alkalinity of a solution is determined by what?
questions.why: Acidity and alkalinity come down to how much free hydrogen is in solution. More free hydrogen means more acidic.

options.t: Total ion count within the solution
options.why: Total ions include those unrelated to pH.

options.t: Ratio of solvent to dissolved solute
options.why: Concentration matters but free hydrogen is the measure.

options.t: Free hydrogen present in the solution

options.why: Temperature affects reactions but not acidity itself.

questions.stem: In a solution, which component is the solvent?
questions.why: The solvent does the dissolving; the solute is what dissolves in it. A solute may be an electrolyte or a nonelectrolyte.

options.t: The substance that dissolves into it
options.why: That is the solute.

options.t: The residue that fails to dissolve
options.why: Undissolved residue is neither solvent nor solute.
That is an ion produced by dissociation.

questions.stem: What is the unit of measurement used for solutions?
questions.why: The milliequivalent is the unit, and one mEq of any cation reacts completely with one mEq of any anion.

options.why: Milligrams measure mass.
Millilitres measure volume.
Moles measure quantity, not reactive equivalence.

questions.stem: What is a cation?
questions.why: Cations are positively charged and are attracted to the cathode in electrolysis. Anions are negatively charged and attracted to the anode.

options.t: An ion with no net charge
options.why: Ions carry charge by definition.

options.t: A molecule that dissolves other substances
options.why: That describes a solvent.
That is an anion.

questions.stem: Which is the main extracellular cation in the body?
questions.why: Sodium is the main extracellular cation — and where the sodium goes, water follows. Potassium is the principal intracellular cation.

options.why: That is the principal intracellular cation.
That acts mainly as a coenzyme.
That is concentrated in bone and teeth.

questions.stem: What proportion of the body's potassium is located inside the cells?
questions.why: 98% of the body's potassium sits inside the cells, which makes it the principal intracellular cation. That is also why serum potassium is a poor reflection of total body potassium.

options.why: That understates the intracellular fraction.
That understates it considerably.
That is far below the actual figure.

questions.stem: Potassium plays a major role in which two processes?
questions.why: Potassium is central to neuromuscular function and to converting glucose into glycogen. Bone growth and clotting belong to calcium; the coenzyme role belongs to magnesium.

options.why: Those are calcium's roles.
That is magnesium's role.
Those are chloride and sodium roles.

questions.stem: Which cation is needed for bone growth, heart function, and blood clotting?
questions.why: Calcium is the principal cation for bone growth, heart function, and blood clotting — three roles worth remembering together.

options.why: That is the main extracellular cation.
That serves as a metabolic coenzyme.
That is the principal intracellular cation.

questions.stem: Magnesium's important role in the body is as what?
questions.why: Magnesium acts as a coenzyme in protein and carbohydrate metabolism. Phosphorus is the one that is a component of ATP.

options.t: A structural component of the ATP molecule
options.why: Phosphorus is the ATP component.
That is potassium.

options.t: A coenzyme in protein and carb metabolism
The main driver of fluid volume
options.why: That is sodium.

questions.stem: Which anion is the determining factor between metabolic acidosis and metabolic alkalosis?
questions.why: Bicarbonate levels determine whether the body is in metabolic acidosis or metabolic alkalosis — which is why it appears on every blood gas you will read.

options.why: That acts as a metabolic coenzyme.
That is a component of ATP.
That regulates stomach pH.

questions.stem: Chloride primarily regulates what?
questions.why: Chloride primarily regulates the pH level of the stomach.

options.why: Calcium and phosphorus govern bone mineralization.
Calcium and potassium govern cardiac excitability.

options.t: The pH level of the stomach

options.why: Sodium is the main determinant of fluid volume.

questions.stem: Phosphorus is identified as an important component of what?
questions.why: Phosphorus is an important component of ATP — adenosine TRIphosphate, which is three phosphates.

options.why: Iron is the key component there.
Cholesterol is the precursor for those.
Collagen is built from amino acids.

questions.stem: The pH scale measures hydrogen ion concentration across what range, and what is neutral?
questions.why: The scale runs 0 to 14 with 7 as the neutral midpoint. Below 7 is acidic, above 7 is basic or alkaline.

options.t: 1 to 14, with 7.4 as the neutral midpoint
options.why: The scale starts at 0 and neutral is 7.

options.t: 0 to 10, with 5 as the neutral midpoint
options.why: The scale runs to 14, not 10.

options.t: 0 to 14, with 7 as the neutral midpoint
0 to 7, with 3.5 as the neutral midpoint
options.why: That truncates the scale at neutral.

questions.stem: What is the normal pH range of the human body?
questions.why: Normal body pH runs 7.35 to 7.45 — a very narrow window. Falling below that range is acidosis; rising above it is alkalosis.

options.why: The lower bound is 7.35, not 7.00.
That range is alkalotic.
That range is severely acidotic.

questions.stem: What happens if the body's pH rises above 7.8?
questions.why: A pH above 7.8 causes uncontrollable, sustained skeletal muscle contractions — the tetany you may see with severe alkalosis.

options.why: The muscular effect is the defining sign.

options.t: Complete loss of skeletal muscle tone
options.why: Alkalosis causes contraction, not flaccidity.
Muscle tetany precedes any cardiac standstill.

questions.stem: What are buffers?
questions.why: Buffers are molecules or compounds that regulate changes in pH — they are the body's defense against swings outside the 7.35 to 7.45 window.

options.why: Those are acids.
Enzymes catalyze reactions rather than buffer them.

options.t: Compounds that regulate changes in pH
Ions that conduct charge in solution
options.why: Ions conduct charge but do not stabilize pH.

questions.stem: Match each electrolyte to its primary role.
questions.why: Four cations and the anions that matter. Sodium and potassium are the extracellular/intracellular pair; calcium covers bone, heart, and clotting; bicarbonate is the acid-base marker.
pairs: Main extracellular cation — water follows it
Bone growth, heart function, and blood clotting
Coenzyme in protein and carbohydrate metabolism
Regulates the pH level of the stomach

questions.stem: Match each term in the enzyme reaction sequence to its meaning.
questions.why: Site, substrate, product is the working order. The enzyme is never consumed — it releases the product and takes on the next substrate.
pairs: The pocket on the enzyme's surface where the reaction occurs
The molecule that fits into the pocket and is acted upon
The new molecule or substance released afterward
A molecule made specifically to stop or slow enzyme activity
